entries.sentence: The NHS lists several possible symptoms: a change in bowel habit, blood in or on the poo, bleeding from the bottom, tummy pain, a lump in the tummy, bloating and weight loss that has no clear reason.
entries.note: NHS symptoms page list as relayed in search summary.

entries.sentence: Tiredness from low iron in the blood (anaemia) can also be a sign.
entries.note: Summary: tiredness from anaemia listed by NHS.

entries.sentence: Many of these symptoms are common and can have other causes, but the NHS says it is important to have them checked by a GP.
entries.note: Summary: some are common and can have other causes, important to get checked.

entries.sentence: Cancer Research UK names bleeding from the back passage, blood in the poo and a change in normal bowel habit as the main symptoms.
entries.note: Search summary of Cancer Research UK page: main symptoms.

entries.sentence: NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a doctor when symptoms last three weeks or more.
A GP appointment is the usual route for non-urgent symptoms.
entries.note: Textbook-level signposting; summary says get checked by a GP.

entries.sentence: Bowel cancer is the name used for both colon cancer and rectal cancer, and treatment decisions depend on where the cancer started.
entries.note: Search summary: both called bowel cancer; treatment depends on where it started (Macmillan staging/colon vs rectal).

entries.sentence: Doctors usually describe how far it has spread using the TNM system.
T covers how far the tumour has grown through the bowel wall, N covers spread to lymph nodes (small glands that help fight infection), and M covers spread to distant organs.
entries.note: Summary: T, N, M definitions; gland definition added in plain words.

entries.sentence: This information is turned into a number stage from 0 to 4.
Stages 1 and 2 are often grouped as early bowel cancer.
Stage 3 means the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes but not elsewhere in the body.
Stage 4 means it has spread to distant organs such as the liver or lungs, and is also called metastatic or advanced cancer.
entries.note: Summary: stage 4 spread to distant organs such as liver or lungs.

entries.sentence: The stage helps the team plan treatment.
entries.note: Summary: treatments offered depend on type and stage (MDT answer).

entries.sentence: At the GP, the NHS and Cancer Research UK describe questions about symptoms, general health and family history.
The GP may feel the tummy and may suggest a rectal examination, where a gloved finger is used to feel inside the back passage.
entries.note: Summary: may feel tummy and ask to do rectal examination; definition added.

entries.sentence: A stool sample or a home test kit called a FIT may be used to look for hidden blood, and a blood test may be requested.
A chaperone, who is a trained health professional such as a nurse, can be requested.
An urgent referral to a specialist does not definitely mean cancer.
entries.note: Summary: urgent referral does not definitely mean you have cancer.

entries.sentence: Colonoscopy is the main hospital test.
A thin, flexible camera looks at the whole large bowel, usually with sedation, and small samples (biopsies) can be taken.
entries.note: Summary: examines whole bowel under sedation; biopsies; camera wording is a plain paraphrase.

entries.sentence: CT colonography uses CT images after the bowel is gently inflated with gas and is used when a full colonoscopy is not possible.
Once cancer is confirmed, CT scans of the chest and abdomen, and MRI for rectal cancer, check for spread.
NHS information says treatment may combine surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted medicines and immunotherapy.
The choice depends on the size and place of the cancer, whether it has spread, genetic changes in it, and the person's age and general health.
Surgery, usually removing the affected piece of bowel, is described by the NHS as giving the best chance of getting rid of the cancer.
entries.note: Summary: surgery best chance of cure (reworded to avoid claim of cure).

entries.sentence: Chemotherapy, medicines that kill cancer cells, may follow depending on stage and health.
entries.note: Summary; definition added in plain words.

entries.sentence: For rectal cancer, radiotherapy or chemotherapy may be given before surgery to shrink the tumour, and sometimes afterwards.
entries.note: Summary of NHS 111 Wales and Macmillan.

entries.sentence: Radiotherapy for rectal cancer is usually combined with chemotherapy, which is called chemoradiation.
Very early colon cancer usually does not need chemotherapy, while stage 1 rectal cancer may need further surgery.
entries.note: Summary: very early colon cancer usually no chemotherapy; rectal stage 1 may need further surgery e.g. TME.

entries.sentence: A team of specialists, including a cancer surgeon, an oncologist, a radiologist and a specialist nurse, usually plans each person's treatment together.
entries.note: Summary: MDT discusses each plan and members.

entries.sentence: A stoma is an opening made on the tummy where part of the bowel is brought to the surface, and waste collects in a bag worn over it.
entries.note: Summary of Macmillan and CRUK pages.

entries.sentence: A colostomy uses the large bowel, and an ileostomy uses the small bowel.
Many stomas are temporary and are reversed later, but some are permanent.
Cancer Research UK says only a small number of people with colon cancer need a permanent stoma, while rectal cancer close to the back passage makes one more likely.
entries.note: Summary of the ileostomy and stoma pages.

entries.sentence: Colostomy waste is usually firmer, and ileostomy waste is looser.
Because more fluid is lost through an ileostomy, drinking enough is important.
Stoma nurses teach how to care for a stoma and help with fitting the bag.
Colostomy UK runs a free helpline, and Macmillan has an online stoma support community.
Bowel habits usually change after surgery.
After a temporary stoma is reversed, Macmillan says it can take several months for the bowel to settle into a more regular pattern, and radiotherapy can slow this.
Some bowel changes after rectal surgery are known as low anterior resection syndrome, and diet changes are often a first step in managing them.
entries.note: Summary: LARS common; UK patient guide suggests diet changes as first step. Name 'low anterior resection syndrome' from search titles.

entries.sentence: Tiredness can last for many months after treatment, according to a hospital trust page.
Bowel Cancer UK has pages on diet after treatment and on emotional wellbeing, with an online forum for peer support.
Check-ups after treatment can include tests such as a blood test for a marker called CEA, to see whether the cancer has come back.
entries.note: Summary: CEA blood test may be done in follow-up.

entries.sentence: Macmillan notes that some effects, such as bowel, bladder or sexual changes, can appear months or years later, and people can raise them with their specialist nurse or cancer doctor.
No. The NHS says many of these symptoms are common and can have other causes.
It still recommends having them checked by a GP.
An urgent referral to a specialist also does not definitely mean cancer.
Tests such as a FIT, colonoscopy or scans help find the cause.
Colonoscopy is usually done under sedation, as the NHS describes it.
entries.note: Summary: examines whole bowel under sedation.

entries.sentence: It looks at the whole large bowel with a thin camera, and biopsies can be taken during it.
Sources put the test at around 20 minutes to an hour.
entries.note: Summary: roughly an hour, one says 20 to 40 minutes.

entries.sentence: Colonoscopy is the main hospital test for bowel cancer, and CT colonography is used when a full colonoscopy is not possible.
Not everyone does. Cancer Research UK says only a small number of people with colon cancer need a permanent stoma.
Many stomas are temporary and reversed later.
Rectal cancer close to the back passage makes a permanent stoma more likely.
Macmillan says the doctor, cancer specialist or nurse explains the treatments and their side effects.
entries.note: Summary: doctor, specialist or nurse explains treatments and side effects.

entries.sentence: Stage is a number from 0 to 4 based on how far the tumour has grown, whether lymph nodes are involved and whether it has spread to distant organs.
Stage 4 is also called advanced or metastatic cancer.
The type and stage help the specialist team decide which treatments to offer. Stage 3 is sometimes called locally advanced.
Specialist nurses and the treatment team support people throughout treatment, according to Macmillan.
Bowel Cancer UK offers information and a peer support forum.
Macmillan notes that national charities such as Bowel Cancer UK offer information and support.
entries.note: Summary: charities offer support and information.

entries.sentence: For stomas, Colostomy UK runs a free helpline and Macmillan has an online community.
Colorectal cancer, colon cancer, rectal cancer
entries.note: Existing aliases; NHS page title 'Bowel cancer'; textbook-level.

entries.sentence: Number stages 0 to 4, built from the TNM system
Colonoscopy, with biopsies taken if needed
A team of specialists, including a surgeon, an oncologist, a radiologist and a specialist nurse
Sometimes needed; many are temporary and reversed later
Radiotherapy or chemotherapy may be given before surgery
May include check-ups and a blood test for a marker called CEA

contradictions: Screening start age differs between retrieved pages (50, 56 and 60 stated for England; 51 for Wales), so no ages were written.
A 2026 screening blog says the England FIT threshold is being lowered; existing entry does not state a threshold, so no conflict, but none written.
Existing entry says 'Early cancers are cured by surgery'; retrieved NHS wording is 'best chance of cure', slightly softer.
